power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: provide a timely checklist for improving the transparency and trust of supervised machine learning (ML) research in psychology.
I strongly endorse this goal and recognize that their focus on retrospective reporting is both valuable and the appropriate scope for an article.
However, I suggest that two related issues warrant greater emphasis in their framework: information leakage and procedural overfitting.
Both can produce optimistic estimates of model performance despite apparently transparent reporting.
I propose two extensions to the checklist: reporting requirements that make information leakage auditable and prospective specification of key analytical decisions through preregistration.
I argue that these additions would further strengthen the ability of readers and reviewers to evaluate the trustworthiness of supervised ML analyses in psychology.

Moreover, comprehensive guidelines that do not sufficiently emphasize these issues may create unwarranted confidence that threats to valid model evaluation have been ruled out, allowing information leakage or procedural overfitting to remain undetected.

"Information" or "data" leakage occurs when information that should be unavailable during model development-most commonly information from test data-directly or indirectly influences model training, preprocessing, feature selection, or other analytical decisions, potentially resulting in an optimistic estimate of out-of-sample performance.

Although the extent of information leakage is not well documented in psychology, evidence from other fields indicates that information leakage caused by data preprocessing is widespread and consequential (Kapoor & Narayanan, 2023).
text.formatted: Although the extent of information leakage is not well documented in psychology, evidence from other fields indicates that information leakage caused by data preprocessing is widespread and consequential <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Kapoor & Narayanan, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Existing applied ML reporting standards, such as REFORMS, also explicitly address leakage and recommend maintaining information boundaries during preprocessing and model development (Kapoor et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Existing applied ML reporting standards, such as REFORMS, also explicitly address leakage and recommend maintaining information boundaries during preprocessing and model development <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Kapoor et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In their article, Min et al. (2026) recognize leakage as a problem, recommending that researchers report whether an independent test data set was used "to avoid data leakage."
text.formatted: In their article, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Min et al. (2026)</ref> recognize leakage as a problem, recommending that researchers report whether an independent test data set was used "to avoid data leakage."

text.text: They also appropriately recommend detailed reporting of preprocessing, feature selection, data splitting, cross-validation, and hyperparameter tuning.
However, determining whether leakage occurred requires knowing not only what procedures were performed but also when, on which data, and within which resampling procedure they were performed.

Although this may have been implicit in Min et al. (2026), preliminary work indicates that few psychology researchers provide accurate enough reporting to assess whether information leakage could have occurred (Radek et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Although this may have been implicit in <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Min et al. (2026)</ref>, preliminary work indicates that few psychology researchers provide accurate enough reporting to assess whether information leakage could have occurred <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Radek et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, I argue that explicit, transparent reporting on what data were used for what preprocessing is vital for such a checklist.
For example, Min et al. (2026) recommend that authors "explain all data-processing procedures and techniques conducted in detail…".
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Min et al. (2026)</ref> recommend that authors "explain all data-processing procedures and techniques conducted in detail…".

text.text: Consider a study reporting that missing values were imputed, continuous variables standardized, features selected, and predictive performance estimated using 10-fold cross-validation.
Although each preprocessing operation has been disclosed, a reviewer still cannot determine whether the performance estimate is valid without knowing where and when those operations occurred.
Were imputation and scaling parameters estimated using the complete data set, on the training data only, before cross-validation or independently within each training fold?
Was feature selection conducted once on the complete data set or on the training data only?

Importantly, the existence of an independent test dataset does not by itself guarantee that leakage has been prevented; this depends on when that set was isolated and whether information from it subsequently influenced data-dependent decisions.
Psychological data additionally create other possibilities for leakage.

Repeated observations from the same participant, or observations clustered within families, schools, clinics, regions, or other units, may require grouped rather than random splitting (Lavelle-Hill et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Repeated observations from the same participant, or observations clustered within families, schools, clinics, regions, or other units, may require grouped rather than random splitting <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Lavelle-Hill et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, longitudinal prediction may require temporal splitting (Roberts et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Similarly, longitudinal prediction may require temporal splitting <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Roberts et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Otherwise, nominally "unseen" observations may contain information closely related to observations encountered during training-inflating evaluation metrics if erroneously interpreted as independent.

Moreover, secondary data may have had subtle transformations applied to it, such as using item response theory for assessment outcomes, before the data even reaches the analysts' hands (Lavelle-Hill et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Moreover, secondary data may have had subtle transformations applied to it, such as using item response theory for assessment outcomes, before the data even reaches the analysts' hands <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Lavelle-Hill et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Authors using secondary data should therefore report whether upstream data transformations could have introduced information leakage across the data boundaries subsequently used for model evaluation.

I therefore suggest extending the logic of Min et al.'s (2026) recommendation to use nested cross-validation to prevent information leakage during hyperparameter tuning to data-dependent preprocessing more broadly.
text.formatted: I therefore suggest extending the logic of <ref type="bibr">Min et al.'s (2026)</ref> recommendation to use nested cross-validation to prevent information leakage during hyperparameter tuning to data-dependent preprocessing more broadly.

text.text: For each data-dependent operation, authors should report which data were used to estimate it (e.g., full data or training only) and whether it was re-estimated within the training data at each stage of resampling.

Authors should also identify and report the unit of generalization (e.g., new students in already-observed schools versus students in entirely new schools) and explain how data dependencies were respected during splitting and resampling.
Procedure --Evaluation and data boundaries.
Report, for each data-dependent preprocessing and modeling operation, which observations were used to estimate or conduct the operation.
Identify the intended unit of generalization and relevant dependencies among observations, and explain how these were accounted for during data splitting and resampling.

A related issue concerns researchers' degrees of freedom in machine learning analyses (Manapat et al., 2024). Min et al. (2026) explicitly recognize ML-specific questionable research practices, including trying different algorithms, hyperparameters, and random seeds and selectively reporting favorable results (Leech et al., 2024; Wigboldus & Dotsch, 2016).
text.formatted: A related issue concerns researchers' degrees of freedom in machine learning analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Manapat et al., 2024)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Min et al. (2026)</ref> explicitly recognize ML-specific questionable research practices, including trying different algorithms, hyperparameters, and random seeds and selectively reporting favorable results <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Leech et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Wigboldus & Dotsch, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Greater transparency is an important response, but retrospective reporting has an inherent limitation: Complete reporting of a final pipeline cannot establish that the pipeline was not selected in response to its observed performance.

Researchers might, for example, explore multiple preprocessing schemes, feature sets, algorithms, hyperparameter spaces, exclusion criteria, random seeds, and performance metrics before "cherry picking" a pipeline that performs particularly well.
That pipeline can subsequently be described transparently, accompanied by open code, and reproduced exactly.

Nevertheless, its apparent performance may still be optimistic because researcher decisions have themselves become part of the optimization process. Yarkoni and Westfall (2017) described this phenomenon more broadly as procedural overfitting, whereby researchers adapt analytical procedures in response to patterns observed in the data. Hofman et al. (2017) used the term human-in-the-loop overfitting to describe the process of repeatedly using the same data to evaluate candidate models.
text.formatted: Nevertheless, its apparent performance may still be optimistic because researcher decisions have themselves become part of the optimization process. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Yarkoni and Westfall (2017)</ref> described this phenomenon more broadly as procedural overfitting, whereby researchers adapt analytical procedures in response to patterns observed in the data. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Hofman et al. (2017)</ref> used the term human-in-the-loop overfitting to describe the process of repeatedly using the same data to evaluate candidate models.

text.text: Importantly, iterative model development is not itself problematic: preprocessing choices, model specifications, and hyperparameters can be explored and compared using training and validation data.
The problem arises when performance on data intended for final evaluation influences those decisions, such that the final evaluation data effectively becomes part of the model-development process.
Thus, even when each individual pipeline is appropriately trained and evaluated, researchers' repeated interaction with the final evaluation data can itself become a source of overfitting.
This distinction presents a fundamental limitation of post hoc transparency.
Even detailed retrospective reporting cannot always establish which analytical decisions were made before results were observed and which were made in response to those results.
I therefore suggest complementing Min et al.'s (2026) retrospective reporting recommendations with prospective specification through preregistration.
text.formatted: I therefore suggest complementing <ref type="bibr">Min et al.'s (2026)</ref> retrospective reporting recommendations with prospective specification through preregistration.

text.text: A framework for doing this with ML already exists. Hofman et al. (2023) developed a two-phase preregistration template designed to preserve the iterative and data-driven nature of ML while protecting final model evaluation.
text.formatted: A framework for doing this with ML already exists. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Hofman et al. (2023)</ref> developed a two-phase preregistration template designed to preserve the iterative and data-driven nature of ML while protecting final model evaluation.

text.text: Phase A, completed before model training and validation, specifies the prediction problem and key analytical choices, including variables, data splitting, transformations, evaluation metrics, and baselines.

Here, researchers should also transparently report prior exploration or analysis of the data by themselves or collaborators that may have exposed them to information relevant to subsequent model development.

Phase B, completed after iterative training and validation but before accessing the test data, specifies the finalized prediction method and training procedure, including cross-validation, hyperparameters, and random seeds.

Researchers therefore retain substantial freedom to develop and optimize models using training and validation data while committing to the final procedure before observing test-set performance (e.g., see Glunz et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Researchers therefore retain substantial freedom to develop and optimize models using training and validation data while committing to the final procedure before observing test-set performance (e.g., see <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Glunz et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: When an independent test set is impractical, for example because of the limited size of many psychological datasets, the same principle could be adapted to nested cross-validation by withholding outer-loop performance from the analyst (e.g., in encrypted or inaccessible files) until the final analytical procedure has been prospectively specified.

I suggest that a supervised ML reporting checklist for psychology should explicitly encourage the use and reporting of such predictive-modeling preregistration frameworks. Min et al.'s (2026) checklist could, for example, require reporting about whether the study was preregistered, provide a link to the preregistration, and require authors to identify and justify deviations from it.
text.formatted: I suggest that a supervised ML reporting checklist for psychology should explicitly encourage the use and reporting of such predictive-modeling preregistration frameworks. <ref type="bibr">Min et al.'s (2026)</ref> checklist could, for example, require reporting about whether the study was preregistered, provide a link to the preregistration, and require authors to identify and justify deviations from it.

text.text: Combining retrospective reporting with prospective specification provides safeguards that neither offers alone.
Transparent reporting establishes what researchers ultimately did; preregistration provides evidence about when key decisions were specified and what information was available when they were made.
Proposed additional checklist item: Open Science.
Report whether key analytical decisions were prospectively specified before final model performance was assessed.

Provide a link to the preregistration(s), where applicable, and report and justify any deviations from it. Min et al.'s (2026) checklist is an important step toward more transparent and reproducible ML in psychology.
text.formatted: Provide a link to the preregistration(s), where applicable, and report and justify any deviations from it. <ref type="bibr">Min et al.'s (2026)</ref> checklist is an important step toward more transparent and reproducible ML in psychology.

text.text: However, I suggest that its goal of increasing trust in machine-learning research could be further strengthened by making two information boundaries more visible to psychologists.
First, analytical information boundaries should be auditable.
Readers need sufficient information to establish not only which preprocessing and modeling operations occurred but also whether evaluation observations could have influenced model development.

Open version-controlled code with timestamps, for example, using GitHub, as recommended by Min et al. (2026), can assist with this assessment, but readers and reviewers should not need to reconstruct analytical information boundaries from code alone.
text.formatted: Open version-controlled code with timestamps, for example, using GitHub, as recommended by <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Min et al. (2026)</ref>, can assist with this assessment, but readers and reviewers should not need to reconstruct analytical information boundaries from code alone.

text.text: Second, researcher information boundaries should be encouraged to be prospectively documented.
A transparently reported final analysis cannot establish whether it was selected after researchers observed the performance of competing alternatives.
Preregistration complements retrospective transparency by providing a prospective record against which subsequent analytical decisions can be evaluated.
Information leakage and procedural overfitting, therefore, share a common principle: credible out-of-sample evaluation depends on the reporting of information flow.

With information leakage, information flows from evaluation data into the analytical pipeline; with procedural overfitting, observed results flow back to researchers and influence the pipeline they subsequently evaluate and report.
Moving forward, reporting guidelines should make the former detectable, whereas prospective specification through preregistration can help constrain and reveal the latter.

Transparency is necessary for trustworthy supervised ML in psychology, but we should be able to establish not only what analysis was ultimately reported but also what information was allowed to influence the process that produced it.
